ONE HUNDRED AND TENTH CONVENTION
THE
annual Convention held in the
110th year of the Psi Upsilon Frater
nity, under the auspices of the Execu
tive Council, w^as called to order at the
Westchester Country Club, Rye, New
York, by Scott Tumer, Phi '02, Presi
dent of the Executive Council, who
after welcoming the delegates, ap
pointed Stephen G. Kent, Delta Delta
11, Secretary of the Executive Council,
as
Temporary Recorder.
Over sixty members of the Frater
nity, delegates and others, attended in
the course of the day.
The Records of the Convention have
been pubhshed in a confidential book
let and have been sent to the Chapters
and the Presidents of the Chapter
Alumni Associations.
One of the most interesting decisions
reached was a resolution the purpose
of which was to broaden the previous
provision of the Constitution so that in
addition to alumni who reside in the
place where a
Chapter is located other
alumni can become active members.
This Vidll be particularly useful in
providing a mechanism for reviving the
active Chapter following the war in
those cases where a
Chapter has no
local alumni.
There have been a number of cases
in the past where it was found desir
able to hold a Convention in New York
under the auspices of the Executive
Council. The first case occurred in 1858.
Then in 1918 and later in 1934 Con
ventions were
again held under the
auspices of the Executive Council. No
Convention was held in 1917, which
was the first and only break in the con
tinuity since 1841, although a
quorum
does not seem to have been present in
the Civil War year of 1862.
The following brothers were elected
to the Executive Council for the usual
term of five years: A. Northey Jones,
Beta Beta '17, LeRoy J. Weed, Theta
'01, and Henry N. Woolman, Tau '96.
At the suggestion of the Executive
Council, the Chapters had appointed
alumni delegates to this and future
Conventions and had also empowered
the Council to appoint delegates for
them in the event that the delegates ap
pointed by the Chapters should be un
able to attend any Convention. This
action was
approved.
An important appointment an
nounced during the Convention was
that of Richard M. Ross, Lambda '20,
President of the Lambda Alumni Asso
ciation, as Archivist.
A resolution was
adopted welcoming
the Epsilon Nu Chapter, which was in
stalled on
April 17, 1943, at Michigan
State CoUege, Lansing, Michigan, into
the Fratemity.
The Executive Council announced
that in January, 1943, a
joint CouncilGovernors Committee on War Prob
lems had been appointed which had
endeavored to advise and assist the
Chapters in their efforts to cope vvdth
the difficulties brought about by the
war.
The Council reported that despite
war conditions, our
Chapters had main
tained a remarkable degree of vitaHty
during the year just concluded. The
annual reports submitted on March 1,
1943, showed an increase of 61 over the
1942 active membership, and a
gain of
16 over the more normal 1941 figure.
This increase was, of course, more than
offset by the increase in those leaving
college, the number of those graduating
and of those leaving without graduat
ing both being considerably larger than
the figures for 1942. The reason for the
increase is indicated by the fact that
more than 82% of those who left col
lege before graduation did so in order
to enter the Armed Forces.

THE LIGHTER SIDE
By Buell A. Patterson, Omega '17
A
"HAVE NOT" became a "Have"
when the Psi Upsilon Convention
of 1943 assembled at Mr. Westchester's
famed Country Club, Rye, New York.
To one who had never attended a con
vention, even at the advanced age
which must be the lot of one who bade
his campus farewell in the original fu
tile attempt to make the world safe for
our American standards, the sessions
were
stimulating. (And mildly, you can
say that again.)
The average undergraduate visits
some other chapters of Psi U during his
collegiate career, and meets brothers
who come to his chapter house from
afar. He meets many of his own almnni
and some from other chapters when
the latter live in his city, but he doesn't
get the over-all picture which makes up
the national significance of Psi Upsilon,
unless he has attended an annual con
vention. He is proud that he is a Psi U,
but doesn't know all the reasons for this
pride. A convention brings out those
reasons.
Brother Peattie, saddled with the
editing of The Diamond, asked the outlander described above to write some
thing in a
light vein about the conven
tion, which should probably be capitahzed, and. Heaven help him and
Brother Peattie, he is almost getting
editorial. The reader's indulgence is
asked while the writer tries to tell of
what made one
delegate that way.
One moming a letter consisting of
illegible hen tracks across a
paper, in
dicating that the paper originated in
the recipient's chapter house, arrived.
Recourse to codes and assistance from
other brothers in the same oflBce devel
oped the fact that the letter was a re
quest to attend the Convention of Psi
Upsilon on
June 19 and to act as one
of four delegates for the outlander's
chapter. Little did they know when
they pledged him and he sat down to
the chapter board that fame and recog
nition was to come to him, even
though
late in life.
More research as to whether those
recurrent letters were t's or I's brought
to hght the names of the other mem
bers of the quartet, and they were con
tacted. They all said, "Well, if you are
going, we will go." No backing out from
responsibihty then, and truly, two out
of the three showed up. At least the
ugly duckling was able to tell them
from club managers, adult caddies, and
their ilk. He was further safeguarded
by insisting that one of them go out on
the train with him after a
too-early
breakfast opposite Grand Central.
There is safety in numbers, misery
loves company or
something, so that
along about noon of convention day,
and directly on the spot where many
a shudder must have been shud in
1929, the two delegates had found the
meeting room, been looked at suspi
ciously, and finally been accepted as
worthy of listening to the words of wis
dom that flowed from the versatile
throat of Brother Scott Turner. Encour
agement came from the fact that, to
the jaundiced eyes of the duo, some
of the delegates looked even more de
crepit and unhealthy than they. Some
actually looked older.
Positive proof than they were at a
convention came, however, only after
committees were
appointed. These
wrangled even as committees always
have, and each had its own
longwinded dissenter. There was
nothing
mysterious about the convention com
mittees which operated just as commit
tees operate under the jurisdiction of

the Rotary Club of What Cheer, Iowa.
Usually the delegate with the loudest
voice wore^ the others down or was

By the time luncheon was served,

discovering more bonds

fore they remembered the time so-andso did something or other and won
dered what ever had become of him.

gate and adding more than fifty hairs

brought recognition where
reserve had been. Good old Joe! The
ice was
breaking, and the little cliques

melting pot of the convention.
Much serious business was transacted
after luncheon, but it was relieved by
just the right seasoning of wisecracks
when some
delegate essayed the role of
a
prophet or dictator, too obviously.
In fact, the frost had gone.
Business over, things became health
ily stimulating (our crutch word), and
the honest pride in Psi U of undergradTHIS

out
acknowledging the excellent work

Delta '39, who has been its editor for

ger, Tau '26, came such feature articles

The desk which I have inherited

uate days was

most sanctimonious. Warren Agry, Zeta
'11, got do'wa to cases with Warren
Agry, Zeta '45, despite the flesh-colored
hair of the senior Agry. The dinner did
it.
Songs started up at table after table,
and even the Kenyonites would have
been impressed. Old friendships really
were renewed and new
friendships
were cemented by the clasped hands
and under the eyes of the Wise Old
Owl.
Just as even a
string comes to an end,
the convention broke up, and the dele
gates headed for home by train or mo
tor car. The brothers told one another
that they sure did like getting together
and certainly must all have lunch to
gether or
stay down for dinner some
night. They ought to meet regularly.
They would. They haven't, but, thank
the Lord, they will always say such
things and always mean them, and
there will be more conventions of the
grand delegates who make up "our be
loved Psi U." You phone me. No, I'U
phone you, dear Brothers in Old Psi U.
Orchids also go to Samuel L. Rosen
berry, Rho '23, Chairman of the Ad
visory Committee, and the Vice-Chair
man, John C. Esty, Gamma '22, who
handled the business and production
of the magazine.
The appointments of brother Esty as
Chairman and brother Eichelberger as
Alumni Editor give me the same con
fidence that would be felt by the foot
ball coach of a small college who sud
denly was
presented with a
pair of

WITH
the ending of the college
year, the possibiUty of maintain
ing even a semblance of normal frater
nity life vanished for most of our
chap
ters. As of March 1, 1943 there were
911 active members, an increase of 61
over 1942. There was an increase of 33
graduating from college over the previ
ous
year. The number of those leaving
college without graduating rose from
271 in 1942 to 423, and of these 82%
entered the armed forces.
The oral reports given by delegates
at the Convention in June are as fol
lows:

The College intends to see that
each fratemity receives sufficient income to
survive the war
emergency including taking
care of interest on indebtedness. The Theta is
receiving favorable treatment. The house,

occupied by 80 men from the Navy unit and
payment wiU be on a
per man basis. There
will be 75 civilian freslimen, and the Chapter

Only two undergraduates remain
in the Chapter. While no contract has as
yet
been signed, the University has orally agreed
to pay a rental for the chapter house which
will carry taxes and $300 for depreciation.
The University will also make minor repairs
and retum the house in a
good state of repair.
Furthermore, rooms in the house will continue
available for any Psi U undergraduates re
maining at the University. The lease will mn
for six months following the end of the war.
Valuable fumiture has been moved and the
University will maintain a
proctor at the
house. A number of alumni have become ac
tive members. There will be an
entering class
of 500. Pledging and initiation will continue.
Sigma�
Only two civilian undergraduates
remain in the Chapter. The Chapter wiU,
therefore, cease
operations as the University,
requires a
fratemity to have ten active mem
bers before permitting it to function.
The University has offered to rent all fra
temity houses, even
though some
may not be
needed, and the Sigma is the only one which
has not yet accepted. In each case the rental

terest if any. The Sigma has no
mortgage and
the University in its case offers only taxes and
insurance. The Chapter has tried to improve
this offer without success and may have to
accept it. No desirable lease to any other lessee

One undesirable feature of the University's

surance (over $1,000 per year) for four or five

main. The house will be closed and fratemity

There are no
college or
interfratemity rules
against initiating new members. The 2,400
Navy students at the College, however, only
take a four months' course, and further initia
tions seem
impractical.

the war, at which time a
refunding operation

administeted by Campus Business Manage
ment and house janitors have been placed on

the armed services. The Chapter's quarters
have been taken over

its overhead has ceased. Its fumiture is in

ing four or five houses on which it holds

as

uates now, but there will probably be only

cendy paid off and the Chicago alumni will

bers in the engineering or medical schools.

come active members if necessary.

erations at the CoUege on

ter house.

ship, but there now remain only six. Finances

ter wiU not continue normal operations.

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL MEETINGS
Meeting of March 23, 1943
A
SPECIAL meeting of the Execu
tive Council was held on March 23,
1943, at the Union League Club, New
York City, with President Scott Turner
presiding. The following members of
the Council were
present: Brothers
Tumer, Burton, ColUns, Jones, Kent,
Morton, Weed and Woolman.
The minutes of the meeting of March
3, 1943, were amended by the inser
tion of a statement recording the pass
ing of a motion commending the WarProblems Committee for the excellent
letter and memorandum sent to the
Chapters.
The Secretary reported that a letter
had gone forward to those Chapters
which had not on March 12th submit
ted their annual reports. He added that
reports had not yet been received from
seven
Chapters.
The Treasurer submitted a list of in
vestments as of March 23, 1943, in the
General, Bridgman and Diamond LifeSubscription Funds.
It was
reported that the March issue
of The Diamond had gone to press.
Brother Morton volunteered to visit
the Epsilon Chapter.
The initiation by the Iota of Profes
sor Wilham Ray Ashford was
reported.
After comments
by the President on
the practice of other fratemities in au
thorizing the use of identification rings
by men in active service, authority was
given him to arrange for the manufac
ture of a suitable Psi Upsilon ring to
be sold only to brothers in active serv
ice in the armed forces.
The desirability of holding the 1943
Convention at a short distance from
New York City was discussed, and the
decision was left within the discretion
of the oflScers.
The President appointed as tellers to
examine, tabulate and count the certifi
cations by Chapters of votes upon the
petition of the Hesperian Society for
the establishment of a
Chapter of Psi
Upsilon at Michigan State CoUege of
Agriculture and AppUed Science,
Brothers Jones, Collins and Kent. This
committee then examined the certifica
tions of chapter-votes on the petition
of the Hesperian Society, and reported
that each of the 27 active Chapters of
Psi Upsilon had voted in favor of grant
ing the petition of the Hesperian So
ciety, in the case of each Chapter by a
favorable vote at a
regular meeting of
the Chapter by at least two-thirds of
its active members at the time when
the vote was taken; that, in the case of
two Chapters, the favorable vote fol
lowed a
prior unfavorable vote, but the
certification of the later favorable vote
was in each case received before all
Chapters had certified to the Executive
Council their votes on the petition; and
that the dates of meetings at which
Chapter votes were taken and the dates
of the certifications of such votes were
as shown on a schedule submitted by
the committee to the meeting.
It was voted that the report of the
special committee be received and that
the committee be discharged. The offi
cers of the Executive Council were con
stituted a committee to make suitable
arrangements for the installation of the
Hesperian Society as a
Chapter of Psi
Upsilon, and to proceed with such instaUation.
The President reported that he had
written to each Chapter announcing the
favorable vote by all Chapters on the
petition of the Hesperian Society, and
proposed to address copies of the final
correspondence to aU the Chapters and
to the Presidents of all Chapter-Alumni
Associations. He submitted a
proposed
telegram to the Phi Alumni Corpora
tion, which was
approved, and exhib
